chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was seated in the circle of Rabi'ah al-Ra'y. A Bedouin came and asked Rabi'ah al-Ra'y about a legal question, and he answered him. When he fell silent, the Bedouin said to him: 'Is it upon your neck?' So Rabi'ah was silent and did not reply anything to him. Then he repeated the question and he answered with the like of that. The Bedouin said: 'Is it upon your neck?' So Rabi'ah was silent.
Then Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'It is upon his neck, or he should not say it; and every mufti is liable.'

key_terms.أَعْرَابِيّ: Bedouin, a nomadic Arab — representing the lay questioner seeking a legal ruling
key_terms.حَلْقَة: Study circle, a gathering of scholars and students for legal discussion
key_terms.رَبِيعَةُ الرَّأْيِ: Rabi'ah al-Ra'y (d. 136 AH), a Medinian jurist known for extensive use of personal reasoning (ra'y) in jurisprudence
key_terms.عُنُق: Neck, used idiomatically in Arabic law to mean personal responsibility and liability
key_terms.مُفْتٍ ضَامِنٌ: The mufti is liable/responsible — a cardinal principle of Islamic legal accountability

ai.seo_question: Is the mufti (fatwa issuer) responsible for the consequences of his rulings in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) was present in the study circle of Rabi'ah ibn Abi Abd al-Rahman — known as Rabi'ah al-Ra'y, a prominent Medinian jurist of the Sunni tradition who relied heavily on personal reasoning (ra'y). When a Bedouin pressed Rabi'ah to confirm legal accountability for his fatwa and Rabi'ah remained silent, the Imam intervened to affirm the principle: anyone who issues a fatwa bears responsibility for its consequences. This incident establishes the foundational Shia jurisprudential principle that a mufti is legally and morally liable for his religious rulings.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Abdul Rahman Bin Al Hajjaj who said,

‘Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> was seated in a circle of Rabi’e Al-Raie, so a Bedouin came over. So he asked Rabi’e Al-Raie a question. So he answered him. So when he was silent, the Bedouin said to him, ‘It is upon your neck’. So Rabi’e was silent from it and did not respond anything over it. So he repeated the question to him. So he answered with similar to that (previously). So the Bedouin said to him, ‘Is it upon your neck?’ So Rabi’e was silent.
So Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> said to him: ‘It is upon his neck, or he should not be saying it; and every Mufti (Fatwa issuer) is responsible’.
en.sarwar: 1. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘Umayr from ‘ Abd al- Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj who has narrated the following: “

Once abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, was in the group of the circle of Rabi‘ah al-Ra’y when an Arab man came and asked Rabi‘ah al-Ra’iy a question and he replied. When he became quiet the Arab man asked, ‘Do you take responsibility for your answer?’ He remained quiet and did not respond. He repeated the question and he gave a similar answer and the Arab man asked, ‘Do you take the responsibility? But Rabi‘ah al-Ra’y remained quiet.
Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, said to him that it is his responsibility. He said, ‘Has He not said that everyone who issues a Fatwa is responsible for it?”’
